content: The fimbria, a component of the female reproductive system, refers to a fringe-like structure of tissue located around the ostium of the Fallopian tube, oriented toward the ovary. It is important to note that the ovary is not directly connected to the adjacent Fallopian tube. During the process of ovulation, sex hormones stimulate the fimbriae, causing them to move in a gentle, sweeping motion toward the ovary. This motion facilitates the release of an oocyte (egg cell) from the ovary into the peritoneal cavity. The cilia present on the fimbriae then work to guide the ovum into the Fallopian tube, where it may encounter sperm for fertilization. Among the fimbriae, only the ovarian fimbria is sufficiently long to make contact with the ovary, playing a critical role in ensuring the oocyte is directed into the Fallopian tube.
